tools.a-constellation-shows-how: A constellation shows how far noise pushes each decision point: the lower Es/N0, the looser the cloud and the likelier a decision error. An eye diagram shows intersymbol interference: the smaller the raised-cosine roll-off β, the narrower the occupied bandwidth, but the longer the pulse tails and the higher the cost of a timing error.

tools.a-series-capacitor-or: A series capacitor or inductor changes only the reactance (sliding along a constant-resistance circle), while a shunt element changes only the susceptance (sliding along a constant-conductance circle). Since the two move in different directions, two elements are enough to push any impedance to the centre. Negative series reactance means a series capacitor; negative shunt susceptance means a shunt inductor.
tools.air-core-coil-inductance: Air-core coil inductance and 3-element Yagi element length estimates.
tools.all-three-prototypes-butterworth: All three prototypes (Butterworth / Chebyshev I / Chebyshev II) are evaluated analytically from their pole and zero positions rather than fitted from tables, so the magnitude, phase and group-delay curves all come from exactly the same transfer function. At the same order, Chebyshev rolls off faster and pays for it with equiripple in the passband or stopband and a more non-linear phase — the trade-off between selectivity and waveform fidelity.

tools.an-ideal-transformer-s: An ideal transformer's turns ratio squared equals its impedance ratio. In practice consider core loss, leakage inductance and frequency range; choose suitable core material and winding for broadband use.
tools.an-l-network-conjugate: An L-network conjugate-matches the load resistance to 50 Ω and removes reflections. For loads below 50 Ω the shunt element is on the load side; above 50 Ω the series element is on the source side. Values assume a pure resistance at resonance — tune out any reactance first.
tools.an-l-network-matches: An L-network matches the load resistance to 50 Ω; computes the inductance / capacitance values.
tools.at-100-modulation-m: At 100% modulation (m = 1) the total power is 1.5× and the sidebands carry only one third of it — the carrier holds no information yet eats two thirds of the power. That is why SSB reaches the same distance on a quarter of the power. m > 1 is overmodulation, and envelope detection will distort badly.

The in-arm configuration decides stopband vs passband: a series LC in a series arm or a parallel LC in a shunt arm → conducts at resonance (band-pass); a parallel LC in a series arm or a series LC in a shunt arm → blocks at resonance (band-stop).

tools.the-amber-dashed-line: The amber dashed line is the optimum sampling instant (the symbol boundary). Every trace converges into two clear level bands there — that is the eye opening. The smaller β, the more the traces interleave everywhere else and the less tolerance there is for clock jitter.
tools.amber-dashed-line-carrier: The amber dashed line marks the carrier ({} fm).
tools.the-amber-hollow-circles: The amber hollow circles are the ideal constellation points (average power normalised to 1). Higher-order modulation carries more bits per symbol but the points sit closer together — the same noise is likelier to cause an error, which is exactly the rate-versus-reliability trade.
tools.the-bandwidth-is-derived: The bandwidth is derived from each component's own frequency behaviour (inductive reactance rises with frequency, capacitive reactance falls), treating the load as frequency-independent. A real antenna impedance varies with frequency, so the figure here is optimistic — best used to compare which matching solution is wider.
tools.the-chart-is-normalised: The chart is normalised to 50Ω: the centre is a perfect match, the upper half is inductive (+jX) and the lower half capacitive (−jX). The dot is the load impedance and can be dragged directly; the blue polyline is the path along which the matching elements push the impedance toward the centre — series elements travel along constant-resistance circles, shunt elements along constant-conductance circles.
tools.the-current-component-set: The current component set does not reach SWR ≤ 2.0 at the centre frequency, so there is no bandwidth to speak of.
tools.the-horizontal-axis-is: The horizontal axis is measured in modulation periods (one period = one full cycle of the modulating signal) and the vertical axis is normalised amplitude; the spectrum's horizontal axis is in units of fm away from the carrier. Everything is computed locally in the browser, with waveform and spectrum updating together.

tools.the-shannon-limit-is: The Shannon limit is Eb/N0 = {} dB: no spectral efficiency can cross it, which is why deep-space links work at extremely low rates. Doubling the bandwidth buys 3 dB of equivalent SNR — the reason spread spectrum and narrow-band weak-signal modes such as FT8 trade time for power.

tools.upload-an-lrpt-recording: Upload a Meteor-M series LRPT pass recording (72k sym/s). It must be a stereo I/Q WAV (left = I, right = Q) at 144 kHz or more — the baseband recorded directly by SDR# and similar software works.
tools.lrpt-takes-a-while: The full chain (demod → Viterbi → RS → JPEG) is compute-heavy; please be patient
tools.lrpt-file-too-large: File too large (about {} MB); the limit is {} MB. LRPT needs the raw 288 kHz stereo I/Q pass recording — trim to just the pass instead of downsampling or mixing to mono.

tools.vna-serial-unsupported: This browser does not support Web Serial (Firefox / Safari); export a .s1p from the instrument software and import it on the left.
tools.vna-range-invalid: The stop frequency must be above the start frequency.
tools.vna-serial-timeout: The device did not respond within 5 seconds: check that you picked the NanoVNA's port, that it is powered on and that no other program is using it.
tools.vna-file-unreadable: The file could not be read: it may exceed the size limit or the browser refused to read it.

tools.vna-err-length: frequency and data line counts differ ({} / {})

tools.fresnel-zone-and-line-of-sight: Fresnel zone and line of sight
tools.fresnel-zone-description: Estimates whether an obstacle intrudes into the first Fresnel zone, including earth curvature; with clearance of at least 60% of the first-zone radius, the loss stays close to free space.
tools.fresnel-enter-valid-values: Enter a valid frequency, distance and heights; the obstacle must lie between A and B
tools.fresnel-verdict-full: Ample clearance: the obstacle is outside the first Fresnel zone, so propagation is close to free space
tools.fresnel-verdict-sufficient: Clearance is adequate: intrusion is under 40%, so the loss stays close to free space
tools.fresnel-verdict-partial: Partly obstructed: the sight line is open, but the obstacle intrudes more than 40% into the first Fresnel zone, adding diffraction loss and fading
tools.fresnel-verdict-blocked: Blocked: the obstacle rises above the sight line, so raise the antennas or change the path; the signal can only travel by diffraction
tools.fresnel-zone-result: Wavelength {} m | first Fresnel radius at the obstacle {} m | at path midpoint {} m
tools.fresnel-bulge-result: Earth bulge {} m | sight-line height {} m | obstacle top incl. bulge {} m
tools.fresnel-clearance-result: Clearance {} m = {}% of the first Fresnel radius (adequate from {}%, fully clear from {}%)
tools.fresnel-margin-spare: {} m of margin above the 60% line (the obstacle could be this much taller)
tools.fresnel-margin-needed: {} m short of the 60% line (raise the antennas or lower the obstacle by this much)
tools.fresnel-horizon-result: Maximum line of sight between the antennas without obstacles ≈ {} km (K = {})
tools.fresnel-assumptions: Use one common datum for all heights. The obstacle is treated as a single knife-edge peak; K = 4/3 is standard atmospheric refraction (use 1 for none). Vegetation, buildings and ground reflection are not included, and diffraction loss is not calculated.
tools.path-profile-description: Paste elevation points along the path to get earth curvature and first-Fresnel-zone clearance at each point, find the tightest spot, and see how much to raise both antennas.
tools.profile-points-hint: One point per line: distance (km), elevation (m), separated by comma, semicolon or space; lines starting with # are ignored. The first line is end A and the last is end B; distances must strictly increase.
tools.profile-error-too-few: At least 3 points are needed: start, end and at least one point in between (with only the two ends the earth curvature cannot be judged, so add the elevation of a midpoint).
tools.profile-error-not-increasing: The distance of point {} must be greater than the previous point's (distances must strictly increase along the path), and its elevation must be a valid number.
tools.profile-error-bad-parameter: Enter a valid frequency, K factor and antenna heights.
tools.profile-error-field-count: Line {} must contain exactly two numbers: distance and elevation.
tools.profile-error-not-number: Line {} contains a value that is not a valid number.
tools.profile-summary: Path length {} km | antenna A altitude {} m | antenna B altitude {} m | wavelength {} m
tools.profile-worst-result: Tightest point: {} km from A, elevation {} m, clearance {} m ({}% of the first Fresnel radius)
tools.profile-raise-result: Raise both antennas together by {} m to reach the 60% clearance line, by {} m for a completely clear first Fresnel zone, or by {} m just to keep the sight line open (0 if already open)
tools.profile-margin-spare: At the tightest point along the whole path there are still {} m of margin above the 60% clearance line
tools.profile-chart-note: Grey is the terrain (earth curvature added), the solid line joins the two antennas, the shaded band is the first Fresnel zone, the dashed line marks 60% clearance and the red dot is the tightest point.
tools.profile-assumptions: Only the given sample points are judged and terrain between them is assumed to have no bumps, so denser sampling is more reliable. Use one datum for heights and elevations; antenna heights are measured above the ground at each end. Vegetation, buildings and ground reflection are not included, and diffraction loss is not calculated.
tools.toroid-winding-description: Works out how many turns a toroid needs for a target inductance, with the rounded-up actual inductance, the factory tolerance range and the wire length; pick a verified manufacturer core or enter your own AL.
tools.toroid-core-hint: Only cores checked against Fair-Rite's official part pages are listed (AL measured at 10 kHz). Common Amidon types (FT-240-43, T-200-2, …) have no source to check against and are not included; choose Custom and enter the AL from your datasheet.
tools.toroid-enter-valid: Enter a valid AL, tolerance (0–100), target inductance and wire diameter

tools.toroid-turns-result.one: Wind {} turn (calculated {}, rounded up so the inductance is never below the target)
tools.toroid-turns-result.other: Wind {} turns (calculated {}, rounded up so the inductance is never below the target)

tools.toroid-actual-result: About {} µH at the nominal AL; {} – {} µH across the factory tolerance
tools.toroid-wire-result: At least {} m of wire (only the length around the core section, no leads)

tools.toroid-window-ok.one: The inner ring holds about {} turn in a single layer: it fits
tools.toroid-window-ok.other: The inner ring holds about {} turns in a single layer: it fits

tools.toroid-window-over.one: The inner ring holds about {} turn in a single layer: it does not fit; wind in layers, use a larger core or thinner wire
tools.toroid-window-over.other: The inner ring holds about {} turns in a single layer: it does not fit; wind in layers, use a larger core or thinner wire

tools.toroid-window-unknown: A custom core has no dimensions, so whether the winding fits is not checked
tools.toroid-one-turn: One turn gives about {} µH; inductance grows with the square of the turns
tools.toroid-note: This is the low-frequency nominal inductance at the AL test condition (10 kHz): ferrite permeability changes with frequency, flux and temperature, so the effective inductance and common-mode impedance at your operating frequency differ, and AL itself carries a ±20–25% factory tolerance. Measure the finished coil. Distributed capacitance and self-resonance are not modelled.
tools.intermod-description: Given several transmit frequencies, lists where their harmonics and 2nd and 3rd order intermodulation products land and flags those inside amateur bands; it also works out the image frequency from a receive frequency and an IF. Handy when tracing RFI and neighbour interference.
tools.intermod-freqs-hint: Separate with commas, semicolons, spaces or new lines; lines starting with # are ignored, repeated frequencies count once, at most 8.
tools.intermod-only-bands: Only show products inside amateur bands
tools.intermod-error-too-many: At most {} different frequencies are supported
tools.intermod-error-invalid: Value {} is not a positive number

tools.intermod-band-count.one: {} of them falls in an amateur band
tools.intermod-band-count.other: {} of them fall in an amateur band

tools.intermod-none-in-band: No product falls in an amateur band. Untick the option above to see all products.
tools.intermod-image-invalid: Enter a valid receive frequency and IF (both must be positive)
tools.intermod-image-high: High-side LO (LO = RX + IF): image {} MHz, {}
tools.intermod-image-low: Low-side LO (LO = RX − IF): image {} MHz, {}
tools.intermod-image-low-none: Low-side LO (LO = RX − IF): the IF is too high, the image would be negative, so there is no such side
tools.intermod-note: Frequencies only, no amplitudes: where a product lands is certain, how strong it is depends on the non-linearity and the power. Harmonics go up to the 5th and intermodulation up to the 3rd order (including three-signal combinations). Whether a product is inside an amateur band uses the site-wide China (ITU Region 3) band table, which stops at 70 cm, so bands from 1.2 GHz up are not flagged. The image depends on whether the receiver uses a high-side or low-side LO, so both are given.
tools.parabolic-dish-description: Works out gain and 3 dB beamwidth from diameter, frequency and aperture efficiency, and focal length, depth and feed position from f/D; you can also measure the depth of an unknown dish to find its focus. For 2.4 / 5.7 / 10 GHz, EME and satellites.
tools.dish-efficiency-hint: Covers feed illumination, surface accuracy, blockage and mismatch losses and has to be estimated by you: 55% is only a typical figure, not a guarantee for any particular dish.
tools.dish-enter-valid: Enter a valid frequency, diameter and f/D; the aperture efficiency must be above 0 and at most 100%
tools.dish-focus-outside: The focus is {} m in front of the aperture plane (outside the bowl, along the pointing direction); put the feed phase centre there
tools.dish-focus-inside: The focus is inside the bowl, {} m behind the aperture plane (deep dish)
tools.dish-focus-on-rim: The focus lies exactly in the aperture plane (f/D = 0.25)
tools.dish-angle-result: The reflector subtends {}° as seen from the focus: the feed pattern has to cover that angle
tools.dish-small-aperture: The aperture is only a few wavelengths across, so the gain formula is no longer reliable here; treat the result as an order of magnitude only
tools.dish-measure-title: Find the focus from a measured depth
tools.dish-depth-hint: Lay a straight edge across the rim and measure the perpendicular distance from the centre of the bowl to it; the diameter is the one entered above.
tools.dish-measure-invalid: Enter a diameter and a depth greater than 0
tools.dish-note: Efficiency is an input, not a result; surface accuracy, feed and strut blockage, offset-fed and dual-reflector designs are not modelled separately and can only be folded into the efficiency. The 70 in 70·λ/D varies between about 65 and 75 with the illumination taper and is not a measured value. Only paraboloids of revolution are handled, with lengths in metres.
tools.waveguide-description: From the size and the filling dielectric: TE / TM cutoff frequencies, single-mode range, guide wavelength, wave impedance, conductor loss, and the attenuation below cutoff (a waveguide-below-cutoff attenuator). EIA WR sizes come from the published waveguide table. Rectangular guides only; no dielectric loss or surface roughness.
tools.rain-fade-description: Rain fade on a terrestrial microwave link: from frequency, polarisation and the 0.01 % rain rate, the specific attenuation, the effective path length, and the fade for any time percentage from 0.001 % to 1 % (ITU-R P.838-3 / P.530-17). It only matters above about 5.7 GHz, and gets worse with frequency.
tools.duty-power-description: Converts peak envelope power (PEP) to average power from the mode's duty factor and the transmit time, for time-averaged RF exposure estimates. Data and worked examples are from FCC OET Bulletin 65 Supplement B (amateur radio). It only averages the power; it does not decide compliance.
tools.ip3-cascade-description: Total gain and total IIP3 / OIP3 of a multi-stage amplifier, attenuator and mixer chain, plus each stage's share of the intermodulation, to find the bottleneck. Enter attenuators, filters and cables as negative gain with the IP3 left empty.
tools.duty-result-duty: Worst-case on-air share of the window {} %, total duty {} %
tools.duty-result-distance: Distance factor {} (multiply the continuous-transmission distances in the OET-65 tables by it)
tools.duty-note: Source: FCC OET Bulletin 65 Supplement B, Table 2 (mode duty factors) and Table 32 (distance conversion). Averaging time is {} minutes for controlled and {} minutes for uncontrolled exposure, and the window slides, so "periodic" takes the worst on-air time in any window. Note: for 2 minutes on / 2 off the bulletin writes 20 minutes in the 30-minute window (it scales the 4 of 6 minutes up), while a strict cycle gives only 16; choose "transmit time within the window" to follow the bulletin's figure. This only averages power and does not decide compliance: that also depends on antenna gain, distance, the band's limit and ground reflection.
tools.duty-error-mode: The mode duty factor must be between 0 and 1
tools.duty-error-time: Times must be valid numbers: window above 0, on-time not negative, pulse width and rate above 0
tools.duty-error-on-longer: The on-time cannot be longer than the window
tools.duty-error-pulse-overlap: Pulse width × rate exceeds 100 %: the pulses overlap
tools.ip3-referred: Which end each stage's IP3 refers to
tools.ip3-total: Total gain {} dB, total IIP3 {} dBm, total OIP3 {} dBm
tools.ip3-limiting: Bottleneck: stage {}, {} % of the total intermodulation
tools.ip3-all-linear: Every stage is passive (ideally linear): there is no third-order intercept; total gain {} dB
tools.ip3-error-gain: Stage {}'s gain is not a valid number
tools.ip3-error-ip3: Stage {}'s IP3 is not a valid number (leave it empty for a passive stage)
tools.ip3-error-empty: At least one stage is needed
tools.ip3-error-finite: Stage {} has a value that is not finite
tools.ip3-note: Formula: 1/IIP3 = Σ G(cumulative before the stage) / IIP3ᵢ (linear milliwatts). The stages' products are added in the worst, phase-aligned case, so the real figure is usually a little better; third-order (two-tone) only, assuming every stage is linear, with no P1dB or noise figure.
tools.waveguide-er: Relative permittivity of the filling εr (air = 1)
tools.waveguide-sigma-hint: Copper 58; aluminium about 35; brass about 15–26 and alloys vary a lot, so use the material certificate.
tools.waveguide-single-mode: Single-mode range {} – {} GHz (up to the next mode's cutoff)
tools.waveguide-propagating: Wavelength in the medium {} mm, guide wavelength {} mm
tools.waveguide-velocity: Phase velocity / c {}, group velocity / c {}, TE10 wave impedance {} Ω
tools.waveguide-multimode: Above the next mode's cutoff: more than one mode will propagate
tools.waveguide-outside-band: Single-mode, but outside the conventional band (too close to cutoff, strongly dispersive)
tools.waveguide-below-cutoff: Below cutoff, nothing propagates: attenuation {} dB/m, or {} dB per cutoff wavelength (2a). Far below cutoff it approaches 54.6 dB per cutoff wavelength.
tools.waveguide-error-size: Sizes must be numbers greater than 0
tools.waveguide-error-height: The inner height b cannot exceed the inner width a (a is the long side)
tools.waveguide-error-er: The permittivity must be between 1 and 100
tools.waveguide-error-freq: The frequency must be greater than 0
tools.waveguide-error-sigma: The conductivity must be greater than 0
tools.waveguide-note: Formulas follow Pozar, Microwave Engineering, chapter 3. Conductor loss assumes a smooth ideal surface, so it is a theoretical floor; real guides (aluminium, unplated) usually lose more, and dielectric loss is not included. Standard sizes and bands come from the published EIA WR table, and the cutoffs agree with its published values (within 0.2 %). The propagation figures are for the dominant TE10 mode only.
tools.rain-rate-hint: The rain rate exceeded for 0.01 % of an average year (1-minute integration). Use ITU-R P.837 data or local weather statistics.
tools.rain-result: Rain fade {} dB (exceeded for {} % of the year)
tools.rain-effective: Path factor r = {}, effective path length {} km
tools.rain-capped: Light rain on a long path: the distance-factor formula breaks down, so the cap of 2.5 is used
tools.rain-warn-freq: Frequency above {} GHz: outside the commonly quoted range, for reference only
tools.rain-warn-path: Path longer than {} km: outside the commonly quoted range, for reference only
tools.rain-error-freq: The frequency must be between {} and {} GHz (the valid range of P.838; 144 / 432 MHz do not apply)
tools.rain-error-dist: The path length must be greater than 0
tools.rain-error-rate: The rain rate must be greater than 0
tools.rain-error-percent: The time percentage must be between {} and {}
tools.rain-note: The P.838-3 coefficients were checked row by row against ITU's official validation data; for P.530-17 (the path factor and the time-percentage scaling) no official validation data was available, so it rests on an open-source implementation and recollection of the text: treat it as an estimate. You must supply R0.01 (the global P.837 rain-rate grid is not built in). Gas absorption, cloud and fog, scintillation and multipath fading are not included.
tools.rain-result-rarest: Exceeded for 0.01 % of the time: {} dB
tools.lora-description: Time on air, receiver sensitivity and link budget (Semtech AN1200.13)
tools.lora-toa-result: Symbol time {} · preamble {} · {} payload symbols · time on air {} · data rate {} bps
tools.lora-link-result: Sensitivity {} dBm · received {} dBm · margin {} dB · max range {} km
tools.lora-invalid-params: Check the inputs: spreading factor 7–12, coding rate 1–4, payload 1–255 bytes, preamble ≥ 6, and the remaining values positive.
tools.lora-note: The formulas follow Semtech AN1200.13, but the official PDF was not retrieved (only cross-checked against a community calculator), so treat it as an estimate. The maximum range is an ideal free-space figure: it ignores earth curvature, terrain, blocking and multipath, and the real reachable distance is far smaller. Compliance: in mainland China, LoRa terminals are "civil metering" micro-power devices, limited to 470–510 MHz and ≤ 50 mW (e.r.p.); 433.05–434.79 MHz is the general micro-power band; 430–440 MHz is the amateur service (secondary, licence required). Follow the current MIIT rules for frequency and power, and do not apply the 868 / 915 MHz used abroad.
